steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our roadmap paper on modeling and simulation, organized around four themes: context, composition, automation, and communication. It should say why simulation studies matter, what the COVID-19 pandemic showed about their current limitations, and list the four goals for further methodological research.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Simulation as a pillar of science; what a simulation study involves
- COVID-19 pandemic: importance of simulation studies and their limitations
- Four goals for methodological research (context, composition/reuse, automation, communication)
- What progress depends on; plan of the paper; Dagstuhl seminar origin

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Simulation as a pillar of science
  - sine qua non in many areas
  - three pillars of science: simulation, empirical evaluation, analytical reasoning (cite)
  - simulation study = intertwined steps: analyze system of interest, develop/refine model, execute experiments, interpret (intermediate) results (cite)
  - process: from research question + system of interest; inputs selected/modified; assumptions and simplifications revised -> suitable abstraction; output requirements specified/adapted; data sources for input, calibration, validation; until useful approximation (cite) (Fig. 1)
  - each step empowered and constrained by methods + modeler's knowledge and experience
  - besides modeler (maybe data analysts, programmers, visualization experts): domain experts, decision-makers involved at various points
- COVID-19 pandemic
  - underlined importance of simulation studies (cite)
  - forecasts (cite); decisions by governments (cite), hospitals (cite), industry (cite), universities (cite)
  - revealed limitations (cite): how quickly useful models can be developed; how results can be interpreted; how results and crucial aspects can be communicated to domain experts, decision-makers, general public (cite)
- Four goals: further methodological research needed
  1. context: helps modelers + domain experts interpret results and reuse simulation products; explain results to decision-makers confidently
  2. model composition and reuse: no building from scratch; saves time; better analysis quality, reuse = incentive for high-quality models
  3. simulation automation: generate central artifacts (models, experiments) automatically; intelligent guidance/support for conducting + documenting; saves time, improves quality
  4. communication: modeler <-> domain expert, modeler <-> decision-makers; central limiting factor for using simulation in decisions; better communication reduces time to impact
- Progress depends on / plan
  - unambiguous, accessible representation of study, activities, sources, products; goal-directed, situation-specific processing of this knowledge
  - next section: state of the art in specifying simulation models (focus discrete, stochastic), simulation experiments, behavioral requirements
  - revisited for research avenues towards the four goals
  - builds on Dagstuhl seminar “Computer Science Methods for Effective and Sustainable Simulation Studies (Dagstuhl Seminar 22401)” (cite)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Simulation is now something many areas cannot do without. Simulation is seen as one of the three pillars of science, together with empirical evaluation and analytical reasoning. A simulation study depends on doing a number of steps soundly and on intertwining them effectively: analyzing the system of interest, developing and refining the simulation model, executing different simulation experiments, and interpreting the results, including intermediate ones. In this process we start from the research question and the system of interest, and then inputs get selected and modified, assumptions and simplifications get revised to choose a suitable abstraction for the model, requirements on the outputs are specified and adapted, and data sources are identified that could be used as input or to calibrate or validate the simulation model, and this goes on until a useful approximation has been achieved (Fig. 1). So each step is empowered by the methods that are used and also constrained by them, and the same is true for the knowledge and experiences of the modeler. Besides the modeler, who may be joined by data analysts, programmers and visualization experts, domain experts and decision-makers might also get involved at different points.

The COVID-19 pandemic recently underlined how important simulation studies are. During the pandemic simulations were widely used to make forecasts and to support decisions by governments, hospitals, industry and universities. Simulations also revealed some current limitations in conducting such studies. These include how quickly useful models can be developed, how the results can be interpreted, and how the results and crucial aspects of simulation studies can be communicated to domain experts, decision-makers and the general public.

- Four goals: further methodological research needed
  1. context: helps modelers + domain experts interpret results and reuse simulation products; explain results to decision-makers confidently
  2. model composition and reuse: no building from scratch; saves time; better analysis quality, reuse = incentive for high-quality models
  3. simulation automation: generate models, experiments automatically; intelligent guidance/support for conducting + documenting; saves time, improves quality
  4. communication: modeler <-> domain expert, modeler <-> decision-makers; central limiting factor; better communication reduces time to impact
- Progress depends on / plan
  - unambiguous, accessible representation of study, activities, sources, products; goal-directed, situation-specific processing
  - next section: state of the art in specifying simulation models (discrete, stochastic), experiments, behavioral requirements; revisited for research avenues
  - builds on Dagstuhl seminar “Computer Science Methods for Effective and Sustainable Simulation Studies (Dagstuhl Seminar 22401)”

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Simulation is now something many areas cannot do without. Simulation is seen as one of the three pillars of science, together with empirical evaluation and analytical reasoning. A simulation study depends on doing a number of steps soundly and on intertwining them effectively: analyzing the system of interest, developing and refining the simulation model, executing different simulation experiments, and interpreting the results, including intermediate ones. In this process we start from the research question and the system of interest, and then inputs get selected and modified, assumptions and simplifications get revised to choose a suitable abstraction for the model, requirements on the outputs are specified and adapted, and data sources are identified that could be used as input or to calibrate or validate the simulation model, and this goes on until a useful approximation has been achieved (Fig. 1). So each step is empowered by the methods that are used and also constrained by them, and the same is true for the knowledge and experiences of the modeler. Besides the modeler, who may be joined by data analysts, programmers and visualization experts, domain experts and decision-makers might also get involved at different points.

The COVID-19 pandemic recently underlined how important simulation studies are. During the pandemic simulations were widely used to make forecasts and to support decisions by governments, hospitals, industry and universities. Simulations also revealed some current limitations in conducting such studies. These include how quickly useful models can be developed, how the results can be interpreted, and how the results and crucial aspects of simulation studies can be communicated to domain experts, decision-makers and the general public.

More methodological research is needed to address these limitations in conducting and communicating simulation studies:

- 1. Ensure that simulation studies come with context. Context is crucial so that modelers and domain experts can interpret results and reuse simulation products. It is also important for explaining simulation results to decision-makers with confidence.

- 2. Improve model composition and reuse. With composition and reuse, models do not have to be built from scratch. This saves time, and it also improves the quality of the analysis, because reuse is an important incentive to design high-quality models.

- 3. Increase simulation automation. Central artifacts of a simulation study, like simulation models and experiments, may be generated automatically. Also, conducting and documenting the simulation study will benefit from intelligent guidance and support. Automation can save the modeler time and contribute to the overall quality of simulation studies.

- 4. Facilitate communication. This means communication between modeler and domain expert and between modeler and decision-makers. Problems in communication seem to be a central limiting factor for using simulation effectively for decisions. Better communication would also reduce the time needed to produce impact.

Progress towards these goals depends largely on representing the simulation study, its activities, sources and products in an unambiguous and accessible way, and on processing this knowledge in a goal-directed and situation-specific way. So in the next section we first look at the current state of the art of how simulation models (focusing on discrete and stochastic models), simulation experiments and behavioral requirements are specified. We come back to these considerations later when we look at promising research avenues towards the four goals we identified. This paper builds on discussions at the Dagstuhl seminar “Computer Science Methods for Effective and Sustainable Simulation Studies (Dagstuhl Seminar 22401)”.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Simulation has become, in many areas, a sine qua non. Simulation, empirical evaluation, and analytical reasoning are regarded as the three pillars of science [1]. Simulation studies rely on soundly conducting and effectively intertwining the steps of analyzing the system of interest, developing and refining the simulation model, executing diverse simulation experiments, and interpreting the (intermediate) results [2]. In this process, starting from the research question and the system of interest, inputs are selected and modified, assumptions and simplifications are revised to choose a suitable abstraction for the model, requirements on outputs are specified and adapted, and data sources are identified that might be used as input or to calibrate or validate the simulation model, until a useful approximation has been achieved [3,4] (Fig. 1). Thus, each step is empowered and constrained by the methods used, as well as by the knowledge and experiences of the modeler. Besides the modeler - possibly joined by data analysts, programmers, and visualization experts - domain experts and decision-makers might become involved at various points.

Recently, the COVID-19 pandemic has underlined the importance of simulation studies [5]. During the pandemic, simulations were widely used to make forecasts [6] and to support decisions made by governments [7,8], hospitals [9], industry [10] and universities [11]. Simulations also revealed some current limitations in conducting such studies [12,13], including how quickly useful models can be developed, how results can be interpreted, and how results and crucial aspects of simulation studies can be communicated to domain experts, decision-makers, and the general public [14].

To address these limitations in conducting and communicating simulation studies, further methodological research is needed:

- 1. Ensure that simulation studies come with context. Context is crucial for helping modelers and domain experts interpret results and reuse simulation products. It is equally important for explaining simulation results to decision-makers with confidence.

- 2. Improve model composition and reuse. Model composition and reuse avoid building models from scratch. This saves time and also improves analysis quality, because reuse is an important incentive for designing high-quality models.

- 3. Increase simulation automation. Central artifacts of a simulation study, e.g., simulation models and experiments, may be generated automatically. In addition, conducting and documenting the simulation study will benefit from intelligent guidance and support. Automation may save time for the modeler and contribute to the overall quality of simulation studies.

- 4. Facilitate communication. This refers to communication between the modeler and domain expert and between the modeler and decision-makers. Problems in communication appear to be a central limiting factor in using simulation effectively for decisions. Better communication would also reduce the time needed to produce impact.

Any progress towards these goals relies largely on an unambiguous and accessible representation of the simulation study, its activities, sources, and products, and on a goal-directed and situation-specific processing of this knowledge. Therefore, in the following section, we first look at the current state of the art in how simulation models (with a focus on discrete and stochastic models), simulation experiments, and behavioral requirements are specified. These considerations will be revisited when we scrutinize promising research avenues toward the four identified goals. The present paper builds upon discussions during the Dagstuhl seminar “Computer Science Methods for Effective and Sustainable Simulation Studies (Dagstuhl Seminar 22401)” [15].
